date: Peter Cooper Hewitt, 1902; HVDC valve on Gotland link, 1954
l1: A sealed tube with a mercury-pool cathode that lets current pass only one way.
l2: An arc forms in low-pressure mercury vapour between a mercury cathode and carbon anodes. Carbon anodes emit few electrons, so current flows only from cathode to anode, rectifying alternating current. A control grid can delay conduction to adjust the output voltage.
l3: Jamin and Maneuvrier observed the effect in 1882; Hewitt invented the rectifier in 1902. Uno Lamm's work at ASEA produced the first practical HVDC valve, in service in 1954 on the Gotland link. The Inter-Island link in New Zealand, decommissioned 1 August 2012, was the last to use them.

confidence.note: Page dates Hewitt's invention 1902 and the first practical HVDC valve 1954.

date: De Forest, patent filed 29 January 1907 (issued 18 February 1908)
l1: A glass bulb with a heated filament, a grid and a plate, where a tiny grid voltage steers a large current.
l2: The grid sits between filament and plate. Because it is close to the filament, a small change in grid voltage changes the plate current more than the plate voltage can. That made the first practical electronic amplifier.
l3: Fleming invented the diode in 1904; de Forest patented the grid design on 29 January 1907 (issued 18 February 1908), and Robert von Lieben independently patented a three-element tube in March 1906. William Eccles coined the name triode around 1920. Transistors replaced it from the 1960s.

confidence.note: Independent invention by von Lieben (March 1906) is stated on the page.

Fun fact: the 'Allied Submarine Detection Investigation Committee' meaning of ASDIC was invented in 1939; no such committee appears in the archives.
